items.sentence: Have you ever *noticed* that dogs are able to smell things that we can’t?
This *is* because a dog’s sense of smell is far more sensitive than a human’s.
For this reason, some dogs *are* specially *trained* to become “sniffer dogs,” which use their keen sense of smell to detect certain items such as hidden drugs.
But this *isn’t* the only task that sniffer dogs can accomplish.
Here *are* a few more interesting ways that these amazing animals can help humans out.
In Pingtung, officials in one park *use* trained dogs to find trees that have “brown root rot” disease.
items.pattern: Prepositional phrase + S + Vt + O + Relative clause (that...)

items.sentence: Due to their keen sense of smell, the dogs *can detect* infected trees.
Once they locate such a tree, they *sit down* beside it until their trainer hands them a treat as a reward.
items.pattern: Adverbial clause (Once...) + S + Vi + Adverbial clause (until...)

items.sentence: Workers then *dig out* these trees before they fall and hurt people.
Since they have realized how useful these sniffer dogs can be, officials in parks across Taiwan *are inviting* them to come and help find the trees with brown root rot disease.
Sniffer dogs’ ability to detect sickness *can be used* for more than just locating sick trees.
items.pattern: Passive: S + be + p.p. + Prepositional phrase

items.sentence: They *have* also *been trained* to predict the onset of certain diseases in humans.
Maria Tello, who was a 58-year-old woman with diabetes, *was* asleep one night.
All of a sudden, her dog Malachi *opened* its eyes and *got up*.
items.pattern: Adverbial phrase + S + Vt +O & / Vi (Compound verb)

items.sentence: By using its powerful nose, it *could sense* that Maria’s blood sugar was dropping to a dangerously low level.

items.sentence: Malachi *woke* her *up* and then *rushed* to get her medicine.
It *turned out* that Malachi saved Maria’s life in this way four more times that year.
How *can* sniffer dogs *manage* to do the above-mentioned tasks?
The answer *is* that diseases cause chemical changes in plants, animals, and even the human body.
These chemical changes usually *create* special odors, and trainers *need* to expose their dogs to these smells many times.
The dogs *are* then *taught* to perform a certain kind of behavior as an alert, such as sitting down or barking, when they come across these smells.
Once their training is complete, sniffer dogs *are assigned* to carry out specific duties.
Dogs really *are* our best friends.
As we continue to understand them better, they *can help* us more.
Who *knows* in what other ways their spectacular sense of smell will be useful to us in the future?

text_genre.raw_text:
This is an expository essay following the structure of Introduction, Body, and Conclusion. Please refer to the Hamburger Structure in the textbook.
The text explores the remarkable abilities of sniffer dogs and how they can be trained to assist humans in various ways. These dogs possess an exceptional sense of smell, far surpassing that of humans. By detecting specific odors associated with diseases, sniffer dogs can identify trees with brown root rot and even predict the onset of illnesses in people, as demonstrated by Maria Tello's dog Malachi. As our understanding of dogs continues to grow, we can anticipate them playing an increasingly important role in our lives.
